lessons.title: Adult Fly Nutrition and Water Needs
lessons.body:
Adult black soldier flies (BSF) do not eat solid food. They have a vestigial mouth and cannot bite or chew. Their only nutritional need is liquid: water and sugar. In the wild, they get this from nectar, honeydew, and rotting fruit juices. In your colony, you must provide this artificially. Without proper nutrition, adults live only 2â3 days and produce few or no eggs. With good nutrition, they can live 5â8 days and lay multiple egg clusters.

Provide a simple sugar-water solution. Mix 1 part white sugar to 4 parts clean water (e.g., 100 g sugar in 400 ml water). Do not use honey, as it can carry diseases. Do not use brown sugar or molassesâthey ferment quickly and attract ants. Change the solution every 2 days to prevent mold and bacterial growth. Use a shallow dish with a sponge or cotton wick so flies can drink without drowning. A small jar with a cotton ball soaked in sugar water works well. Place it in the adult cage, but away from egg-laying sites to avoid contamination.

Water alone is not enough. Flies need sugar for energy to fly, mate, and lay eggs. In hot African climates, dehydration is a major killer. Provide additional plain water in a separate shallow dish with stones or sponges for flies to stand on. Never leave open waterâflies will drown. In dry seasons, mist the cage lightly once a day with a hand sprayer. Avoid soaking the cage; high humidity encourages mold.

You can also offer overripe fruit like banana, mango, or papaya. Mash it and place it on a small plate. Flies will feed on the juices. This is a good supplement but not a replacement for sugar water. Remove fruit after 24 hours to prevent fruit flies and odors. In summary, adult BSF need constant access to clean sugar water and plain water. Check and refill daily. This small effort dramatically increases egg production.

lessons.title: Mating and Egg-Laying Behavior
lessons.body:
Mating in black soldier flies happens in flight. The male hovers and grabs the female mid-air. This requires space, light, and warmth. In small cages, mating is often poor. For good results, use a cage at least 1.5 m tall and 1 m wide. Place it outdoors under a roof or in a greenhouse with natural sunlight. Mating peaks in the morning, from 8 am to 11 am, when sunlight is bright and temperature is between 25Â°C and 30Â°C. Below 20Â°C, mating stops. Above 35Â°C, flies become inactive.

Provide a vertical structure for males to perch and display. A piece of cardboard or a hanging strip of shade cloth works. Males also need a lekâa group of males competing for females. So keep at least 50â100 adults in the cage. A sex ratio of 1 male to 1 female is ideal. If you have too many males, they harass females and reduce egg-laying. Too few males, and many females remain unmated.

After mating, females look for a narrow crevice to lay eggs. They lay in clusters of 200â600 eggs. In nature, they lay near decaying organic matter. In your colony, provide artificial egg-laying sites. Common designs: a piece of corrugated cardboard folded like an accordion, or a wooden block with 2â3 mm wide grooves. Place these near the top of the cage, in a shaded spot. Females prefer dark, tight spaces. A small plastic container with a lid and a 5 mm slit also works. Put a little moistened chicken feed or fruit pulp near the slit to attract them.

Females lay eggs in the late afternoon, from 3 pm to 6 pm. After laying, they die within 1â2 days. Collect eggs daily, preferably in the evening. If you leave eggs too long, they hatch and larvae crawl away. Also, other flies or ants may eat them. With proper conditions, a healthy colony can produce 1â2 grams of eggs per day per 1000 adults. Thatâs enough to start a new larvae bin every day.

lessons.title: Collecting Eggs Efficiently
lessons.body:
Collecting eggs is the most important daily task in BSF farming. If you miss a day, you lose a whole generation. Eggs are tinyâabout 1 mm long, white to cream-colored, laid in tight clusters. You need a simple, repeatable method. Use corrugated cardboard or wooden blocks with grooves as egg traps. The grooves should be 2â3 mm wide and 5â10 mm deep. Females insert their abdomen into the groove and lay eggs. You can also use a plastic container with a lid and a 5 mm slit, but cardboard is cheaper and works well.

Place the egg traps in the adult cage in late afternoon, around 3 pm. Put them in a shaded area near the top, where females prefer to lay. Add a small piece of overripe fruit or a dab of moist chicken feed near the trap to attract them. Leave the traps overnight. In the morning, check for egg clusters. They look like small white patches inside the grooves. Use a soft brush or a small spoon to gently scrape the eggs into a clean container. Do not use your fingersâyou will crush them.

Collect eggs every morning. If you wait until afternoon, larvae may hatch and crawl away. Also, ants and other predators can destroy the eggs. Once collected, place the eggs in a small plastic cup with a lid. Keep them at room temperature (25â30Â°C) and out of direct sunlight. They will hatch in 3â4 days. You can also put the egg trap directly into a new larvae bin. The larvae will hatch and start feeding on the waste. That saves handling.

For efficiency, set up a rotation. Have two sets of egg traps. Use one set in the cage, and clean the other. In the morning, swap them. This way, you always have fresh traps ready. Record how many grams of eggs you collect daily. A good colony produces 1â2 grams per 1000 adults per day. If production drops, check nutrition, temperature, and density. Clean traps with water and dry them before reuse. Never use soapâresidue kills eggs.

lessons.title: Monitoring Adult Fly Health
lessons.body:
Healthy adult flies are active, fly readily, and have intact wings. Sick or stressed flies sit on the cage floor, have crumpled wings, or die within 1â2 days. Monitoring health helps you catch problems early. Check your colony daily. Look for these signs: flies that cannot fly, flies with deformed wings, or many dead flies. A few dead flies per day is normalâadults live only 5â8 days. But if you see 20% or more dead at once, something is wrong.

Common health issues include dehydration, starvation, and poisoning. Dehydration happens when water is missing or the cage is too hot. Provide fresh water daily. Starvation happens when sugar water is not available or is too old. Change sugar water every 2 days. Poisoning can come from pesticides, cleaning chemicals, or moldy food. Never use insecticides near the cage. Clean the cage with plain water and a brush, not soap or bleach. If you see mold on food or egg traps, remove it immediately.

Also watch for predators and parasites. Ants are the biggest enemy. They enter the cage and eat eggs and young larvae. Place the cage legs in small containers of oil or water to create a barrier. Geckos, spiders, and birds can also eat adult flies. Use mesh small enough to keep them out. Mites can infest flies, but this is rare in well-managed colonies. If you see tiny moving dots on flies, increase ventilation and reduce moisture.

Keep records. Write down daily temperature, humidity, number of dead flies, and egg production. A simple notebook works. If egg production drops, compare with previous weeks. Often, the cause is obvious: a heat wave, a missed feeding, or a new cleaning product. By monitoring, you can fix problems before they wipe out your colony. Healthy adults mean more eggs, and more eggs mean more larvae to turn waste into protein.

lessons.title: Managing Adult Fly Density
lessons.body:
Overcrowding is a silent killer in BSF colonies. Too many adults in a small cage leads to stress, poor mating, and low egg production. As a rule, allow 1000 adults per cubic meter of cage space. For example, a cage 1 m x 1 m x 1.5 m has a volume of 1.5 mÂ³, so it can hold about 1500 adults. If you have more, either expand the cage or harvest some adults. You can also release excess adultsâthey will not survive long in the wild, but they may find mates and lay eggs elsewhere.

Signs of overcrowding include: flies constantly bumping into each other, many flies sitting on the floor, and few mating pairs. Also, egg production drops because females cannot find quiet spots to lay. In severe cases, flies die faster due to heat stress and lack of food access. If you see these signs, reduce density immediately. Remove some adults by opening the cage briefly and letting them fly away, or use a vacuum to catch and transfer them to another cage.

To maintain ideal density, start with fewer adults and let them age naturally. Adults live 5â8 days, so if you add 200 new adults every day, you will quickly exceed capacity. Instead, add new adults only when the old ones die. A simple method: count the number of dead flies you remove each day. If you remove 200 dead flies, you can add 200 new pupae or newly emerged adults. This keeps the population stable.

Also, provide enough space for vertical flight. Males need to hover to mate. A tall cage is better than a wide, short one. If space is limited, use multiple smaller cages rather than one crowded cage. Each cage should have its own food and water stations. Never mix different age groups in the same cageâyoung flies may be disturbed by older ones. With proper density, your flies will be calm, mate well, and lay plenty of eggs.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Adult Fly Issues
lessons.body:
Even with good care, problems happen. Here are common issues and quick fixes.

Problem 1: No mating. Check temperature. Below 25Â°C or above 35Â°C, mating stops. Move cage to a warmer or cooler spot. Ensure enough lightâmating needs bright, indirect sunlight. If cage is too small, flies cannot fly properly. Use a taller cage. Also, check sex ratio. Too many males harass females. Aim for 1:1. If you have mostly males, add more females.

Problem 2: No eggs. Females may be unmated, or egg-laying sites are wrong. Provide proper egg traps: corrugated cardboard or grooved wood, placed in a shaded area. Add a little moist chicken feed near the trap. If females are old (over 8 days), they may be too weak to lay. Replace with young adults. Also, check nutritionâsugar water must be fresh and available.

Problem 3: Flies dying quickly. Usually dehydration or starvation. Provide fresh water and sugar water daily. In hot weather, mist the cage. If many flies die within 24 hours of emergence, they may have been poisoned by pesticides or mold. Clean the cage with plain water and remove any moldy food. Also, check for predators like antsâuse oil barriers on cage legs.

Problem 4: Eggs eaten or missing. Ants are the main culprit. Set up ant barriers. Also, collect eggs every morning before they hatch. If you see tiny larvae in the egg trap, you waited too long. Remove the trap and put it in a larvae bin. If other flies (house flies) are in the cage, they may eat BSF eggs. Keep the cage clean and use fine mesh to exclude them.

Problem 5: Larvae not hatching. Eggs may be too dry or too wet. Keep eggs at 25â30Â°C and moderate humidity. If you store them in a sealed container, open it daily for air. If eggs turn brown or black, they are dead. Start with fresh eggs from healthy females. With these fixes, most problems resolve in a few days. Keep records to spot patterns.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: BSF Adult Fly Management

In black soldier fly (BSF) farming, the adult stage is the shortest and most capital-efficient phase of production â but only if you manage it deliberately. Adults live roughly 5â9 days, do not feed in the conventional sense, and exist almost entirely to mate and lay eggs. For an African agribusiness, this means adult management is not a biology lesson; it is a productivity lever. Every egg you fail to collect is lost larval biomass, lost feed conversion, and lost revenue from frass, protein meal, and live larvae sales.

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into field-ready guidance for small and medium BSF operations in Africa â from Nairobi and Kampala to Accra, Lagos, and Kigali. It assumes you are running a cage-based or netted breeding system, possibly in a converted greenhouse or shade structure, and that your main constraints are heat, humidity, dust, and unreliable power for climate control.

1. Adult Fly Nutrition and Water Needs

Adult BSF do not have functional mouthparts for feeding on solid food. They rely on stored fat reserves from the larval stage and take only water. In hot African conditions â 30â35 Â°C in many lowland areas â dehydration is the leading cause of premature adult death. Provide clean water in shallow dishes with a sponge, cotton wick, or gravel to prevent drowning. Change water daily; stagnant water breeds bacteria and fungus. If your cage is in a dry region (e.g., northern Ghana, Sahelian zones), consider misting the cage walls once or twice daily.

2. Mating and Egg-Laying Behavior

Mating is triggered by bright light â ideally natural sunlight or strong artificial light (â¥ 1000 lux). In tropical Africa, outdoor or semi-outdoor cages perform best. Flies lek (gather in swarms) around a visual marker such as a hanging string, branch, or dark vertical object. Egg-laying occurs in narrow crevices near an attractant substrate â typically decomposing organic waste or a bait of fermented fruit. Place egg traps (corrugated cardboard, wood slats, or plastic strips) within 10â20 cm of the attractant. Females lay 500â900 eggs per batch.

3. Collecting Eggs Efficiently

Egg masses are small (2â5 mm clusters) and easily missed. Use fine-mesh trays or corrugated strips that can be removed and inspected. Harvest twice daily â morning and late afternoon â to prevent larvae hatching inside the cage. Label each batch with date and cage ID. Weigh egg mass to estimate yield (1 g â 20,000â30,000 eggs). Move eggs to a nursery tray with moist feed within 24 hours.

4. Monitoring Adult Fly Health

Healthy adults are active, fly readily, and cluster near light and water. Warning signs: sluggish movement, wing damage, high mortality before day 4, or low egg output. Track daily mortality, sex ratio (aim for 1:1), and egg hatch rate. Poor hatch rate often indicates inbreeding, temperature stress, or poor larval diet in the previous generation.

5. Managing Adult Fly Density

Overcrowding reduces mating success and egg output. A practical rule: 10,000â15,000 adults per mÂ³ of cage volume, with a maximum of 20,000 in well-ventilated tropical cages. Sex ratio should be balanced; too many males waste space and stress females. Separate cages by generation to avoid inbreeding and to maintain genetic vigor.

6. Troubleshooting Common Adult Fly Issues

Common problems in African BSF operations include: no mating (usually light or space issue), no eggs (wrong attractant or no crevices), high mortality (heat, dehydration, or poor larval diet), and mite or ant infestation (hygiene and physical barriers). Address root causes rather than symptoms.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Pesticides and Adult Fly Mortality

Never use residual insecticides, mosquito coils, or agricultural pesticides near adult BSF cages. Adult flies are highly sensitive to pyrethroids, organophosphates, and fumigants. Even drift from nearby crop spraying can wipe out an entire breeding colony within hours. If you must treat pests in adjacent areas, use physical barriers, sticky traps, or biological controls â and always wash hands and tools before entering the cage. In shared compounds, communicate with neighbours before any spraying.

  • â Record daily mortality, sex ratio, and egg yield in a simple logbook.

Business takeaway: In African BSF farming, adult fly management is the bottleneck that determines your weekly egg supply â and therefore your larval output, your feed sales, and your frass revenue. Treat the adult cage as a production asset: monitor it daily, keep records, and never let heat, dehydration, or pesticide drift silently destroy your colony.

quiz.q: What do adult black soldier flies eat?
options: A) Solid food like fruit pulp
C) Sugar water and plain water
quiz.explanation: Adult BSF cannot eat solid food; they need liquid sugar and water.

quiz.q: How often should you change sugar water for adult flies?
quiz.explanation: Changing every 2 days prevents mold and bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What is the ideal sugar-to-water ratio for adult BSF?
options: A) 1 part sugar to 1 part water
B) 1 part sugar to 4 parts water
C) 1 part sugar to 10 parts water
D) 2 parts sugar to 1 part water
quiz.explanation: A 1:4 ratio provides enough energy without being too thick.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using honey in sugar water?
options: C) Flies do not like it
quiz.explanation: Honey can contain pathogens that harm flies.

quiz.q: What happens if adult flies do not get enough water?
quiz.explanation: Dehydration quickly kills adult BSF, reducing lifespan and egg production.

quiz.q: When does mating peak in black soldier flies?
quiz.explanation: Mating is most active in bright morning sunlight.

quiz.q: What temperature range is best for BSF mating?
quiz.explanation: Mating stops below 20Â°C and above 35Â°C; 25â30Â°C is ideal.

quiz.q: What is a lek in BSF behavior?
options: A) A type of egg trap
B) A group of males competing for females
quiz.explanation: Males form leks to display and compete for mates.

quiz.q: What is the ideal sex ratio for adult BSF in a cage?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 ratio balances mating opportunities and reduces harassment.

quiz.q: Where do female BSF prefer to lay eggs?
quiz.explanation: Females seek tight, dark crevices to lay egg clusters.

quiz.q: What is a common artificial egg-laying site for BSF?
quiz.explanation: Corrugated cardboard provides the narrow grooves females prefer.

quiz.q: When do female BSF usually lay eggs?
quiz.explanation: Egg-laying peaks from 3 pm to 6 pm.

quiz.q: How many eggs can a female BSF lay in one cluster?
quiz.explanation: A typical egg cluster contains 200â600 eggs.

quiz.q: How often should you collect BSF eggs?
quiz.explanation: Daily collection prevents hatching and predation.

quiz.q: What tool is best for scraping BSF eggs from traps?
quiz.explanation: A soft brush gently removes eggs without crushing them.

quiz.q: How long do BSF eggs take to hatch?
quiz.explanation: Eggs hatch in about 3â4 days at 25â30Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a healthy adult BSF colony?
options: A) Flies sitting on the floor
quiz.explanation: Healthy flies are active, fly readily, and mate.

quiz.q: What is the biggest predator of BSF eggs in a colony?
quiz.explanation: Ants invade cages and eat eggs and young larvae.

quiz.q: How can you prevent ants from reaching the adult cage?
options: A) Use oil barriers on cage legs
C) Leave food on the floor
quiz.explanation: Oil or water barriers on legs stop ants from climbing.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold in the adult cage?
quiz.explanation: Mold can poison flies and should be removed promptly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended density of adult BSF per cubic meter?
quiz.explanation: 1000 adults per mÂ³ prevents overcrowding stress.

quiz.q: What is a sign of overcrowding in a BSF cage?
options: A) Flies constantly bumping into each other
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding causes stress and poor mating.

quiz.q: How can you reduce adult fly density without harming the colony?
quiz.explanation: Releasing excess adults lowers density and stress.

quiz.q: Why is a tall cage better than a short, wide cage for BSF?
options: B) It allows vertical flight for mating
quiz.explanation: Males need vertical space to hover and mate.

quiz.q: What should you do if your BSF are not mating?
quiz.explanation: Mating requires proper temperature (25â30Â°C) and bright light.

quiz.q: What can cause adult flies to die within 24 hours of emergence?
quiz.explanation: Pesticides or mold can quickly kill newly emerged adults.

quiz.q: What should you do if eggs turn brown or black?
options: A) They are ready to hatch
quiz.explanation: Brown or black eggs are dead and will not hatch.

quiz.q: How can you tell if BSF eggs have hatched too early?
options: A) You see tiny larvae in the egg trap
quiz.explanation: Tiny larvae indicate eggs hatched and should be moved to a bin.

quiz.q: What is a good record to keep for adult fly management?
options: A) Daily temperature and egg production
quiz.explanation: Recording temperature and egg yield helps spot problems early.

quiz.q: What should you do with overripe fruit offered to adult flies?
options: A) Leave it for a week
quiz.explanation: Removing fruit after 24 hours prevents mold and fruit flies.
